Punish
PUN-ish
v.t.
From Latin punire, to inflict penalty, from poena, penalty, pain. Webster 1828: to pain, to afflict with pain, loss, or calamity for a crime or fault. Scripture reserves the word almost entirely for God’s own act as Judge, and for the magistrate acting under Him.

Biblical Definition

Punish in Scripture is chiefly what God does, and the striking thing about the biblical use is where He begins. Amos states the principle that governs the whole prophetic literature: You only have I known of all the families of the earth: therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities (Amos 3:2). The therefore is the shock. Nearness to God is not an exemption from judgment but the ground of it, and the same logic runs through judgment must begin at the house of God (1 Peter 4:17). Isaiah widens it to the whole world and names the target precisely: I will punish the world for their evil, and the wicked for their iniquity; and I will cause the arrogancy of the proud to cease, and will lay low the haughtiness of the terrible (Isaiah 13:11). Zephaniah reaches men whose offence is not violence but settled indifference: I will search Jerusalem with candles, and punish the men that are settled on their lees: that say in their heart, The LORD will not do good, neither will he do evil (Zephaniah 1:12). Wine left on its dregs grows thick and flat, and the figure describes a man too comfortable to expect anything from God at all — and God searches for him with lamps.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines PUNISH as to pain; to afflict with pain, loss, or calamity for a crime or fault; primarily to afflict with bodily pain, but extended to any penalty inflicted by authority for the violation of law.

expand to see more

PUNISH, v.t. — To pain; to afflict with pain, loss, or calamity for a crime or fault.

To inflict a penalty on, by authority, for the violation of a law, whether human or divine.

Punishment is inflicted by the offended party or by lawful authority; revenge is taken by a private person, and is forbidden.

To chastise; as, a father punishes his child for disobedience — though here the end is correction rather than retribution.

From Latin poena, penalty — the root also of penal, penalty, penance, and pain.

Key Scripture

Amos 3:2 — "You only have I known of all the families of the earth: therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities."

Isaiah 13:11 — "And I will punish the world for their evil, and the wicked for their iniquity; and I will cause the arrogancy of the proud to cease, and will lay low the haughtiness of the terrible."

Zephaniah 1:12 — "And it shall come to pass at that time, that I will search Jerusalem with candles, and punish the men that are settled on their lees: that say in their heart, The LORD will not do good, neither will he do evil."

Proverbs 11:21 — "Though hand join in hand, the wicked shall not be unpunished: but the seed of the righteous shall be delivered."

Modern Corruption

Modern religious sentiment has largely retired the idea that God punishes at all, reassigning every judgment to natural consequence, and the therapeutic reframing of sin as harm rather than guilt removes the only category in which punishment makes sense.

expand to see more

The consequence-only account — that God does not punish but simply allows sin to work its own ruin — has the appearance of mercy and the substance of a denial. It cannot survive Isaiah 13:11, where God says I will punish and then names what He will do to the arrogancy of the proud, nor Amos 3:2, where the punishing follows from the knowing. It also empties the cross. If God does not punish sin, then the death of Christ was not a bearing of penalty, and penal substitution collapses into a demonstration of solidarity. The doctrines stand or fall together: a God who does not punish needs no propitiation, and a Saviour who bore no penalty saves from nothing.

The second and subtler corruption redefines sin as harm. Where the primary moral category is damage done to another person or to oneself, an act with no measurable victim ceases to be sin, and God’s interest in it becomes unintelligible. Scripture’s category is guilt before God: David, who had committed adultery and arranged a murder, says Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight (Psalm 51:4). He does not mean Uriah was unharmed; he means the offence that requires atonement is offence against God. Zephaniah 1:12 shows how far this reaches — men who had harmed no one, settled on their lees, saying in their hearts that the LORD would do neither good nor evil, and God searching the city with candles to find them.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew paqad (H6485), to visit, to muster, to punish; naqam (H5358), to avenge; Greek kolazo (G2849), to punish, to chastise; ekdikeo (G1556), to vindicate, to punish judicially.

expand to see more

Hebrew paqad (H6485) — to visit, to attend to, to punish; the same verb covers God’s visiting in mercy and in judgment (Amos 3:2; Exodus 20:5).

Hebrew naqam (H5358) — to avenge, to take vengeance; reserved to God and to the magistrate He appoints.

Greek kolazo (G2849) — to punish, to correct; the Lord knoweth how… to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be punished (2 Peter 2:9).

Greek kolasis (G2851) — punishment; these shall go away into everlasting punishment (Matthew 25:46).

Greek ekdikeo (G1556) — to execute justice on behalf of; the root of the magistrate’s office in Romans 13:4.

Usage

"You only have I known… therefore I will punish you (Amos 3:2) — nearness to God as the ground of judgment, not exemption from it."

"I will cause the arrogancy of the proud to cease (Isaiah 13:11) — the named target of the world’s punishment."

"Punish the men that are settled on their lees (Zephaniah 1:12) — God searching a city with candles for the comfortably indifferent."
